_: Texts on the page that are the author's own wording as applied (typos fixed, see dev/build/typos_V1.0.x.json): the rewrite list counts them as done. One entry per release that applies rewrites.
V1_0_22: a clue in the puzzle isn't valid

Not the same shape. If a link would make both sides of the delta the same shape (two identical polyominoes for example), it makes it impossible. This means it should be walled. This is also true if we know what shape a side would be without knowing its position (an area number 2 is always a domino, no matter where it goes).
Must grow. If one side of the delta is decided and the other side matches it currently, we know it must grow at least one more tile.

Same size. If a side is known to be size 4, then the other side is size 4 as well. This check is also used to know what the maximum size for a shape next to a gemini can be, if the total area is 8 then that shape will be size 4 at best.
Same shape. A polyomino on one side gives its shape to the other side. This also applies if the shape isn't finished : a shape on one side contains a 1x4? the other side needs one too.

Same shape advanced. When a side is known to contain a unique shape (for example it has a 2x3 and it won't be able to make another one), if the other side also contains that shape we know it is exactly that instance. We can then test rotations/symmetry using this point as the common point, which is fast to test as there are at most 8.

Sizes push each other. Since the smallest size is 1, the big size of an inequality is always at least two. Chains like a < b < c will make c at least 3. This also means if c is known to be size 3, then b is size 2 and a is size 1.
Loops can't exist. A link that would make a loop of a < b < a is impossible, so the solver puts a wall there. This is also true with bigger loops like a < b < c < a.

Room for whole chains. When a chain of inequality exists, we know the area it will take will be at least n(n+1)/2 (1+2+3...+n). If the area needed to hold it is too small it would break, so we can't place wall in places that would force a chain to be too restrained.

Size across the wall. Since size needs to be strictly positive, a known 2 next to a difference 2 makes the other side size 4. We don't even need for exact size to use this idea, if a shape is known to be between size 2 and 4 and it hits a difference 5, the other side must be between size 7 and 9.

Odd and even. An odd difference makes one side odd and the other even and an even difference makes both sides odd or both sides even. We can use this idea to eliminate links that would create parity issue without having to check for all possible sizes.
Two numbers, two pieces. If a piece touches two difference walls with one being 2 and the other being 4, the other side of those walls can never connect, no matter what the original piece does.

The numbers must fit. Adding numbers up should always be lower than the total area. if a wall would make that area too small it is a link. For example a 6 and a 4 can't be inside a size 8. This is also used to know that two area numbers with the same number must connect if their sum is bigger than the total area (two 5 must be together in an area 9).

No tile left over. In a similar idea, if the sum of all the numbers is EXACTLY equal to the area (with no way to merge two number together), then every tile must link to an area number. this is especially useful for far away tiles, since we now know they must connect to one of the area numbers.

Counting. Since every type appears once per piece, two pieces with a rose in common are walled off instantly. Uneven counts are impossible so a wall that would force uneven count is a link. This also makes puzzle with global uneven count get rejected instantly.

Counting Advanced. The extension of the uneven counting, narrow passages must be passed through if they would leave uneven count, this also works for slightly bigger passages if the difference of rose amount is bigger to the same degree. A 2 wide passage with three red one blue on the left and three blue one red on the right must have the passage linked to allow the connection for 2 shapes.
Who goes with whom. Similarly to a Flow puzzle, the solver lists every way to group the remaining roses into pieces. Pretty useful when puzzle has a lot of different roses in small packs.

Must fit the shape. The piece has the polyomino's size, it is also considered like an area number. Also tiles already together must fit in the shape. So if a shape has no line of length 3, two tiles in a row instantly get a wall at both ends.

Where the polyomino can go. The solver tests each place the shape can go over the polyomino, if in every universe two shapes must be linked they are linked (same with walls). This helps identify that two identical polyominoes where the merge causes all possible tiling to fail must be different pieces.
1 and 4. A 1 links all the tiles round the corner, a 4 walls them all. Pretty trivial :)

2 and 3. A 2 is exactly two walls, either in a bend or a straight line. So if two walls or two links are decided we know the other two states. A 3 is more tricky, as it can be three walls, or four if one piece wraps around the corner. When no piece can wrap (too small, or no way round), a 3 with three walls known links the fourth.

Edges of puzzle. A 1 or a 2 at the edge of the puzzle is respectively a link or a wall. Similarly a 1 or a 3 at an inward corner is two links or two walls. And more is impossible. (this is also true for walls the solver discovers midway)

Count the sides. If a palisade has already enough links or walls known, the solver can instantly input the rest. With a straight 2 palisade with a wall already known bottom of it, the solver puts the wall on the opposite side, and two links on the left and right directly.
Size of the piece. A tile with k open sides is in a piece of at least k + 1 tiles, 0 needs 5 tiles, 1 needs 4... So if a 1 Palisade has an area number 3 neighboring, it can't link.

Fake walls. A piece can't pass directly through a bend palisade or a dead end palisade. If a bunch of dead end palisades are in a row the solver knows a piece can't pass through it. (two bends are an exception)

Palisades together. Palisade can have some interesting interaction when next to each other, or when diagonally adjacent. Most famous example of that is the 1 palisade and 2 palisade diagonally adjacent forces the 1 to have two links outwards. There are other cases specially with solitude that the solver can use.

Only two pieces. When a puzzle is known to have EXACTLY two shapes in total, palisades become a very good tool to find coloring reasoning. For example no matter the orientation, the opposite side of a straight line palisade will always be the same piece/color.

A count is a limit. With a 2 east compass, nothing three columns or more to the east can join the compass. This also walls off 0 compasses instantly. If walls force a detour, it can also reduce the "reachable" even more.

The only way. If a compass needs a lot of tiles and one of them is a choke point that leads to the count being possible, it must be linked. This is very important to know when a compass has to "wrap around". Similarly to polyomino, if in every possible compass shape two tiles are linked/walled, we can add that. (this is mostly useful for compass with all 4 direction inputted)

Size. Size of compasses are ranges, but we can find some easy truths : A compass with four numbers cap the piece at 1 + N + E + S + W tiles. And any compass also gives a smallest size at "biggest number + 1" (the compass tile itself).

Count doesn't match. A compass with north 3 cannot merge with another compass above it if they also have north 3. This logic is also true with the first compass being north 2, or the second compass being further away. In the opposite manner, if a tile needs to be part of two compasses, mostly from size being too big, then the two compasses must be together in the same shape.
Grow and stop. If a shape hasn't satisfied the precision yet, and has only one way out, then it must grow out that way. Similarly if it has already satisfied the precision then it's walled off.

The board must divide advanced. Knowing that the board must divide everything equally, when a choke point exists we can count to know how many tiles need to be poking out/in. A pocket of size 23 with precision 5 needs to be poking out through its only choke point 2 tiles.
Sizes that fit. An area of size 7 with Minimum 3 can only use pieces of size 3, 4 or 7: a 5 or a 6 would leave 2 or 1 tiles and fail the minimum.

Too small. Similarly to precision, if a shape has only one way out and hasn't satisfied the minimum, it has to grow that way. This also makes us know a closed area with the size strictly under twice the minimum is one piece, two pieces wouldn't fit.

Together with the other bound. A Minimum and a Maximum make a range: Knowing that can help reduce possible size combinations even more, sometimes it can even rule out a size completely. min 4 max 6 in a pocket of 12 can only be 4+4+4 or 6+6.

Too big together. When adding up two shapes size make a number above the maximum, then those two shapes must be distinct. And in puzzles where the total amount of shape is known or limited (mismatch for example) maximum allows the solver to enumerate all possible shapes and plan accordingly.
Sizes. Since every piece is a shape in the shape bank, they must all have one of their size. If the bank only holds shape of size 2 and 5, a closed area of size 9 forces the 2+2+5 combination.
Where a shape can go. With shape bank every possibility is very restrictive, so testing all possible placement is a good strategy specially with small shape banks.

What is in common. If every bank shape contains a 2x2 block, so does every piece. This means a straight corridor must go out in a way that allows it to contain that 2x2. This is also true if every shape doesn't contain a 2x2, but it is taken care of by the point above.

Enough shapes. Mismatch is a piece amount limitation, since there is 1 domino, 2 trominoes, 5 tetrominoes... so with a size limitation we can easily tell what pieces HAVE to be used, in particular a puzzle which area is equal to the total size of all shapes must have room for every, single, one.
A shape is used once. Since every shape is unique, if they are already drawn, every piece that looks like it must grow to avoid breaking mismatch.
Room for the neighbour. If an area can be filled with a shape that would leave the remaining hole of that same shape, then it can't happen, as both would be matching and break mismatch.

A shape is used once advanced. The solver doesn't need to check if the shape is fully drawn to know if that shape is still available in the rest of the puzzle. If two places need to be of area 3, since there exist only 2 trominoes, the rest of the puzzle can't be either of those and no size 3 can happen.

One size. If the puzzle is one shape, then the puzzle has one size. This means the shape can only be one size that divides the total area of the puzzle. If the puzzle is of size 12, then the shape can't be of size 5.

One shape for every group. Every part of the puzzle that is known can act as small pocket of knowledge about the shape as a whole. If we know the shape contains a 1x3 and the 2x2 then it must be of size 5 or more.

One shape for every group advanced. This idea of pocket of knowledge can be pushed further, if we know from a compass that the shape must fit inside a 5x5 square as a whole, then finding the correct shape can get a lot easier as any shape that breaks that size limit are instantly dismissed without testing the tiling. Combining known sub-shapes that must fit inside the true shape and size limitation from puzzle grid or clue we can go through all possibilities very quickly.
Neighbours lose a shape. When a piece is already decided, every neighbor that looks like it must grow, this is especially useful with small shapes like the 1x1, or with shape bank.

Two shapes. And when only two possible shapes are used in the puzzle, we know the solution must always alternate, like a checkerboard pattern. This also makes us know a corner can't have exactly 3 walls.
Neighbours lose a size. Exactly the same idea that mingle shape had, but even more restrictive, if a shape is decided neighbouring shapes of the same size must grow.
Two sizes. And exactly like mingle shape, with only 2 sizes the solution is also a sort of checkerboard pattern, so all corners of exactly 3 walls are banned.
One symbol each. Since N symbols make N pieces, this rule allows us to know the total amount of pieces. Also two neighbouring pieces that each already hold a symbol can't merge and are walled off.
Reaching a symbol. A group with no symbol must grow to one, so a wall that would cut it off from all of them is a link and a closed area with one symbol needs to be one piece.

Fill the box. Tiles known to be one piece need to fill everything in the middle to be a rectangle, so an L tetromino needs to be a 2x3. The solver doesn't need to know the tiles are already linked for that, knowing they will eventually be part of the same shape is enough to fill the whole middle.

Walls run straight. At every corner, there can never be exactly 2 walls that form a bend, otherwise the other two links would create a bend tromino. This means every corner either runs straight, has 3 walls, or has 4 walls. (or 0)

What placement fits the size. When a piece's size is known, it's very fast to check every placement of it with boxy as the amount of possible rectangles is very small. This is done to know what link is always there and what wall is always there.

Prime sizes. To go further, when the size of a piece is known and is a prime number then the shape is a strip: a size of 7 is always a 1x7, and finding way to fit it into the puzzle often leads to knowing if it is horizontal or vertical.
At least 3 tiles. Title says it all ! The 1x1 and 1x2 are both rectangles, so non boxy is also minimum 3 so minimum logic also applies.
Keep growing. If a shape is currently a rectangle, it has to grow no matter what. And if it only has one way to grow then that needs to be a link.
Three walls. If we know three walls at a corner, we know the 4th is a link, pretty self explanatory.

Poking-in corners. Where two walls meet at a right angle pointing into the board (or from a hole), the tile diagonal to it has to join one of its two neighbours. If it didn't, it would instantly create 4 walls. Two pieces (or holes) with touching corners are impossible. This helps reduce possible placement for polyomino and such.
Two colors. Since no corner has exactly three walls (a T), so every corner has 0, 2 or 4 walls. This also makes the final puzzle 2 colorable, with the outside being one of them.
